title: Content-Safety System · Praxis AI
summary: Raised content-moderation accuracy from 49.6% to 80.8% on a 10,000-case internal benchmark, with a policy graph that gives every decision a traceable policy basis.
myRole: I own the content-safety system from requirements to launch. That covers the data and evaluation framework, the model context, fine-tuning and deployment of the classifier, decision thresholds, and the policy graph that connects each decision to the rule behind it.

caseStudy.problem: A moderation model has to catch violations without flooding reviewers with false alarms, and every allow, review or block decision has to point to the policy that justifies it. The starting point was 49.6% accuracy on the 10,000-case internal benchmark, which left both too many missed violations and too many false positives.

decisions.title: Improve accuracy on four fronts at once
decisions.detail: Accuracy rose through four coordinated changes: fine-tuning on human-verified golden data, a redesigned model context, a rebuilt data and evaluation framework, and tuned decision thresholds. The result reflects all four together, so none of them is credited on its own.

decisions.title: Keep policy separate from model scores
decisions.detail: A Neo4j policy graph links clauses, risk categories, scope and allow/review/block rules. It is kept separate from model scores and versioned by effective date, so a decision can be traced to the policy in force when it was made, and policy can change without retraining the model.

decisions.title: Evaluate reproducibly, with a holdout
decisions.detail: A reproducible evaluation pipeline covers 10 domains and 14 scoring categories, with development/holdout separation, error analysis and safety checks. Every change is scored against the same fixed data.

decisions.title: Ship only verified models
decisions.detail: I fine-tuned Gemma 12B with PEFT/LoRA on GCP Vertex AI A100s and released it as versioned artifacts. SHA-256 checks block any model file that does not match its recorded version from being served.

evidence.claim: Content-moderation accuracy rose from 49.6% to 80.8% on the 10,000-case internal benchmark.
On the same benchmark, missed violations fell by 73% and false positives by 96.9%.
Violation-detection F1 reached 0.865 on a 4,000-case holdout drawn from the benchmark.

tradeoffs: Thresholds trade missed violations against false positives. Reporting both rates alongside accuracy keeps that choice visible instead of hiding it in one number.
Separating the policy graph from model scores adds versioning work, but it lets reviewers change a rule, or check which rule applied on a given date, without touching the model.
The holdout is drawn from the same benchmark, so it measures generalization within that benchmark's domains and categories. New policy domains need their own evaluation.

outcomes: Content-moderation decisions now rest on a measured classifier and an explicit, versioned policy basis.
Model releases cannot be served unless their artifacts pass integrity checks.
Evaluation runs reproducibly across 10 domains and 14 scoring categories, so later changes can be compared with this baseline.
